answer.answer: Yes. Coverage J pays business interruption loss, contingent business interruption loss and extra expenses when computer systems are interrupted for longer than the waiting period by a security failure (such as a ransomware attack) or a systems failure. On this quote J has a $1,000,000 limit, a $2,500 retention and an 8-hour waiting period (1 hour for a denial of service attack when a panel DDoS vendor is used). Lost income is capped at a 180-day indemnity period and excludes lost profit from loss of market or other consequential loss, and the client must file a sworn proof of loss within 90 days of discovery, so confirm they understand those conditions.

answer.answer: Yes. Breach response costs cover the costs to notify affected individuals and up to two years of credit or identity monitoring for people affected by a data breach, and this quote shows a $1,000,000 limit with a $2,500 retention for it. Costs must be incurred with our prior written consent and within one year of discovering the breach, so the agent should remind the client to get consent before spending. Notification costs are generally tied to a data breach, so the client should confirm that patient or other personal information was actually affected.

answer.answer: Yes. Network and Information Security Liability (II.A) pays claim expenses and damages when a claim is made against Icon Dental for a security failure, data breach, or privacy liability, and the carrier has the right and duty to defend a claim seeking damages payable under the policy. It is a claims-made-and-reported coverage, so the suit must first be made and reported during the policy period (or an extended reporting period), and the $2,500 retention applies before the carrier pays claim expenses. Defense costs also erode the limit, and the agent should confirm the incident falls after the retroactive date and is not excluded (e.g., prior knowledge).

answer.answer: Generally no. The policy excludes any loss arising out of a physical event or natural disaster, and flood is named specifically. Cover is also tied to a security failure or systems failure, and systems failure is defined to exclude loss of or damage to physical equipment or property. Computer Replacement and Bricking responds only to loss of firmware integrity from a security failure, so it would not pick up flood-damaged hardware. If the client has a separate property or equipment breakdown policy, that is where the hardware loss would belong; the agent should confirm what the client has.

answer.answer: Generally no. The policy excludes electrical or mechanical failure or interruption of a utility or other third party, including blackouts, brownouts, power surges and outages, so a lost day from a power company outage is not covered. The only carve-back is for business interruption where the loss arises directly from a service provider experiencing its own security failure, which a plain power outage is not. Also, business interruption only applies when the interruption lasts longer than the waiting period (8 hours on this quote, or 1 hour for a DDoS with a panel mitigation vendor), so the agent should confirm the cause of any outage.

answer.answer: Yes, if the malware is a security failure that causes a loss of firmware integrity in hardware the practice owns or leases. Computer Replacement and Bricking (II.M) pays the reasonable and necessary cost to restore or replace that hardware, and it is on this quote with a $1,000,000 limit and a $2,500 retention. The tangible property exclusion carves this coverage out, so it does not block it. The agent should confirm the laptops are owned or leased by the practice, that the damage is firmware-related, and that written consent is obtained from the carrier before spending. Employee-owned devices not used for business are not a security failure.

answer.answer: It depends on whether the phone was used for the practice's business. The definition of security failure excludes failures of computers, peripherals or mobile devices owned or leased by an employee and not used for the business operations of the named insured. If the phone was used for business (for example, practice email or patient information), the hack can count as a security failure, and mobile devices are listed in the definition of computer systems. Note that computer systems are devices operated by you on your own behalf, so the agent should confirm how the phone was used and whether the practice's data or systems were affected.
